The cancer detection system integrates at least two imaging systems that use different imaging modalities, with each system generating sampled image data from the tissue under examination. A dedicated modeling unit is provided for each modality. These modeling units generate corresponding modeled image data based on a common set of biophysical parameters, enabling the different modalities to be analyzed within a unified framework.

A joint non-linear inversion module combines information from the modality-specific modeling units to reconstruct a set of joint biophysical properties. By integrating complementary information from multiple imaging modalities, the module can provide a more comprehensive characterization of the examined tissue than any single modality alone.

The system also includes a scaling unit that updates or revises the common biophysical parameters based on the reconstructed joint biophysical properties. The revised parameters are then used by the modeling units to generate updated modeled image data. A comparator evaluates the differences between the sampled image data and the corresponding modeled image data for each modality. If the differences fall below a specified threshold, the reconstructed biophysical properties may be accepted as sufficiently accurate. If the threshold is not met, the parameters may be revised again and the modeling, inversion, and comparison steps repeated until an acceptable level of agreement is achieved.
outputs.L4:
The cancer detection system combines sampled data acquired from multiple medical imaging modalities, such as magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, ultrasound, positron emission tomography, or optical imaging. Because each modality measures different aspects of tissue structure or function, the sampled images may differ in resolution, contrast, noise level, and physical interpretation. The system registers the images to a common spatial reference and represents them using a shared set of biophysical parameters associated with tissue properties, such as cellular density, vascularity, perfusion, metabolism, or mechanical characteristics.

For each modality, a forward model predicts the image that would be produced by a proposed distribution of the shared biophysical parameters. Although the modality-specific models may use different measurement equations, they remain coupled through those common parameters. The system then performs a joint nonlinear inversion to estimate parameter values that are simultaneously consistent with all available imaging data. Information from one modality can therefore constrain ambiguities or compensate for limited sensitivity in another.

The reconstruction proceeds iteratively. Starting from an initial parameter estimate, the system generates modeled images for the respective modalities and compares them with the corresponding sampled images. The resulting differences, or residuals, are used to update the shared parameters. Iterative scaling may normalize the contributions of the modalities, account for differences in units and dynamic range, and prevent a single data source from disproportionately controlling the reconstruction.

This process continues until the differences between the modeled and sampled images fall below a selected threshold, the parameter updates become sufficiently small, or another convergence criterion is satisfied. The final output is a spatially consistent set of joint biophysical-property estimates and, optionally, reconstructed images, confidence measures, or maps highlighting tissue regions with features associated with malignancy.

By interpreting multimodal observations through a unified physical model rather than evaluating each image independently, the system may provide a more coherent characterization of suspicious tissue. The resulting joint property maps can support cancer detection, lesion localization, treatment planning, or longitudinal monitoring, subject to clinical validation and review by qualified medical professionals.

## The Power of “The”

“The” is one of the smallest yet most important words in the English language. Known as the definite article, it points to a specific person, place, object, or idea. When we say “the book,” we usually mean a particular book that is already known or understood.

Although “the” may seem insignificant, it makes communication clearer. Compare “I saw a dog” with “I saw the dog.” The first sentence refers to any dog, while the second identifies a specific one. This simple distinction helps speakers and writers express their meaning precisely.

The word also appears in countless names and expressions, such as “the Sun,” “the Internet,” and “the best day of my life.” Quietly and almost invisibly, “the” connects ideas and gives them focus. Its frequent use shows that even the shortest words can have an essential role in language.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the architecture of a cancer detection platform that compares measured images with modeled images and updates common biophysical parameters until the difference falls below a threshold.
counterfactuals.output:
## Architecture overview

The platform is an **inverse-modeling system**: it estimates tissue properties by repeatedly generating modeled images and adjusting biophysical parameters until those images agree sufficiently with measured patient images.

```text
Measured images
      │
      ▼
Preprocessing and registration ──────────────┐
      │                                      │
      ▼                                      │
Biophysical parameter initialization         │
      │                                      │
      ▼                                      │
Forward model / image simulator              │
      │                                      │
      ▼                                      │
Modeled images                               │
      │                                      │
      ▼                                      │
Measured–modeled comparison                  │
      │                                      │
      ├── Error ≤ threshold ──► Results and cancer assessment
      │
      └── Error > threshold ──► Parameter optimizer ──► Forward model
```

### 1. Image acquisition and preprocessing

The input may be MRI, CT, ultrasound, PET, microscopy, or multimodal images. The preprocessing layer:

- corrects scanner artifacts and intensity nonuniformity;
- denoises and normalizes image values;
- segments the organ or region of interest;
- aligns images to a common coordinate system;
- estimates image noise and acquisition uncertainty.

Registration is important because the comparison assumes that measured and modeled pixels or voxels represent the same anatomy.

### 2. Shared biophysical parameter model

The system defines a common parameter vector, for example:

\[
\theta =
[\text{cell density},\ \text{proliferation rate},\ \text{diffusion},
\ \text{perfusion},\ \text{oxygenation},\ \text{vascular permeability},
\ \text{mechanical stiffness}]
\]

“Common” means the same parameters drive all modeled image channels. For example, perfusion may affect both dynamic contrast MRI and PET predictions, allowing several measurements to constrain one physiological estimate.

Parameters may be:

- global for the patient;
- regional for a lesion;
- spatial fields varying voxel by voxel;
- hierarchical, with population priors and patient-specific values.

Bounds and physiological priors prevent implausible solutions.

### 3. Forward biophysical model

The forward model predicts tissue state from the current parameters. It may combine:

- tumor growth and invasion equations;
- nutrient, oxygen, or drug transport;
- vascular flow and contrast-agent kinetics;
- tissue mechanics;
- an observation model converting tissue state into expected scanner signals.

Conceptually:

\[
\hat I_m = F_m(\theta, A_m)
\]

where \(\hat I_m\) is the modeled image for modality \(m\), \(F_m\) is its forward model, and \(A_m\) contains acquisition settings such as resolution, timing, and scanner response.

The observation model should reproduce effects such as point-spread function, voxel sampling, and noise so that simulated and measured images are comparable.

### 4. Image comparison and objective function

A comparison engine computes a discrepancy between measured images \(I_m\) and modeled images \(\hat I_m\):

\[
J(\theta)
=
\sum_m w_m D_m(I_m,\hat I_m)
+ \lambda R(\theta)
\]

Here:

- \(D_m\) may be mean-squared error, normalized correlation, mutual information, or a likelihood based on the modality’s noise model;
- \(w_m\) balances modalities or image regions;
- \(R(\theta)\) imposes smoothness, physiological constraints, or prior knowledge;
- \(\lambda\) controls regularization.

A spatial residual map can show where the model fails to explain the measured data.

### 5. Parameter-update loop

If the objective or residual exceeds the acceptance threshold, an optimization engine updates the shared parameters:

\[
\theta_{k+1} = U(\theta_k,\nabla J,\text{constraints})
\]

Possible update methods include gradient descent, adjoint-based optimization, Gauss–Newton methods, Bayesian inference, evolutionary algorithms, or surrogate-model optimization.

Each update triggers another forward simulation and image comparison. The loop terminates when:

- discrepancy falls below a predefined threshold;
- parameter changes become negligible;
- a maximum iteration or runtime limit is reached;
- validation metrics indicate divergence or non-identifiability.

Convergence should reflect expected image noise rather than an arbitrary demand for exact pixel agreement.

### 6. Cancer assessment and outputs

After convergence, an interpretation layer uses the fitted parameter maps, residuals, and image-derived features to produce:

- lesion probability or malignancy score;
- tumor extent and spatial parameter maps;
- estimated biological characteristics;
- confidence or credible intervals;
- model-fit quality and out-of-distribution warnings;
- optional longitudinal growth or treatment-response forecasts.

The fitted parameters themselves do not automatically establish cancer. A validated classifier or clinical decision rule must map them to a cancer assessment, and the output should support—not replace—radiology and pathology review.

### 7. Supporting platform services

A production system also needs:

- **Data layer:** DICOM/PACS integration, metadata, versioning, and de-identification.
- **Compute layer:** GPU/CPU scheduling, parallel simulation, caching, and model surrogates.
- **Model registry:** Versioned forward models, parameter definitions, and calibration data.
- **Auditability:** Complete records of inputs, preprocessing, iterations, thresholds, and outputs.
- **Validation:** External cohorts, scanner-specific calibration, subgroup testing, and prospective clinical studies.
- **Security and governance:** Access control, encryption, monitoring, and regulatory-quality change management.

In short, the architecture couples a patient-specific **digital biophysical model** to an iterative optimizer: measured images constrain shared physiological parameters, the forward model converts those parameters into synthetic images, and residual error drives updates until a statistically and clinically justified stopping criterion is reached.

counterfactuals.output:
## Title

**Systems and Methods for Multimodal Medical Image Reconstruction Using Forward Modeling and Joint Nonlinear Inversion**

## Abstract

A system and method are disclosed for reconstructing a spatial representation of a subject from sampled measurement data acquired using two or more distinct medical imaging modalities. For each modality, a modality-specific forward model relates one or more shared and/or modality-specific model parameters to predicted measurement data in a measurement domain. The sampled measurement data, predicted measurement data, model parameters, residuals, objective-function terms, or updates are scaled to place contributions from the respective modalities on mutually comparable numerical bases. A joint objective function is formed from discrepancies between the sampled measurement data and the predicted measurement data for the respective modalities, optionally together with one or more regularization, constraint, prior, or coupling terms. A nonlinear inversion engine iteratively updates the model parameters to reduce the joint objective function. One or more convergence criteria are evaluated during the iterative inversion. Upon satisfaction of a convergence criterion, the system outputs a reconstructed spatial representation, quantitative parameter map, diagnostic image, or other characterization of the subject.

## Exemplary Specification Language

### Technical Field

The present disclosure relates generally to medical image processing and, more particularly, to systems and methods for jointly reconstructing or estimating anatomical, physiological, functional, biochemical, mechanical, electrical, acoustic, optical, or molecular characteristics from measurement data acquired by multiple medical imaging modalities.

### Summary

In one aspect, a multimodal medical imaging system includes an input interface configured to receive respective sampled datasets acquired from a subject using at least a first medical imaging modality and a second medical imaging modality distinct from the first medical imaging modality. The system further includes one or more processors configured to apply respective modality-specific forward models to a set of model parameters, thereby generating predicted datasets corresponding to the respective sampled datasets.

The set of model parameters may include one or more shared parameters that influence the predicted datasets for multiple modalities, one or more modality-specific parameters, or combinations thereof. The processors scale at least one of the sampled datasets, predicted datasets, residuals, objective-function components, model parameters, gradients, Jacobians, Hessians, or parameter updates. The scaling may compensate for differences in physical units, dynamic ranges, sample counts, noise characteristics, spatial resolutions, conditioning, or information content among the modalities.

The processors form a joint objective function based at least in part on discrepancies between the sampled datasets and corresponding predicted datasets. The joint objective function is minimized, maximized, or otherwise optimized by a joint nonlinear inversion process that iteratively updates the set of model parameters. During the inversion, the processors evaluate one or more convergence criteria. When at least one termination condition is satisfied, the processors generate an output representing at least one property of the subject.

The output may include a reconstructed image, a fused image, a spatial distribution of a tissue property, a quantitative parameter map, a segmentation, a classification, an uncertainty map, a confidence value, or data suitable for display, diagnosis, treatment planning, intervention guidance, or longitudinal monitoring.

### Detailed Embodiment

For modality \(m\), acquired measurement data may be represented by \(y_m\), and a modality-specific forward operator may be represented by:

\[
\hat{y}_m = F_m(x_s,x_m;\theta_m),
\]

where \(\hat{y}_m\) denotes predicted measurement data, \(x_s\) denotes one or more parameters shared across modalities, \(x_m\) denotes one or more modality-specific parameters, and \(\theta_m\) denotes known or estimated acquisition, calibration, geometry, physics, or instrument parameters.

A joint objective function may be expressed as:

\[
\Phi(x_s,\{x_m\}) =
\sum_{m=1}^{M} w_m D_m(S_m y_m,S_m\hat{y}_m)
+\sum_{r=1}^{R}\lambda_r R_r(x_s,\{x_m\}),
\]

where \(M\geq2\), \(S_m\) is a scaling or normalization operator, \(D_m\) is a modality-specific discrepancy measure, \(w_m\) is a weighting coefficient, and \(R_r\) is a regularization, prior, constraint, or cross-modality coupling term.

The discrepancy measure may comprise a least-squares metric, weighted least-squares metric, robust loss, likelihood function, negative log-likelihood, Poisson data-fidelity term, Gaussian data-fidelity term, Rician data-fidelity term, Kullback-Leibler divergence, or another statistical or deterministic measure.

The scaling operator may be predetermined or adaptively calculated. For example, scaling may be based on a norm, variance, noise covariance, estimated signal-to-noise ratio, number of samples, sensitivity matrix, Jacobian magnitude, Fisher information, objective-function magnitude, gradient magnitude, or combinations thereof. Scaling may be updated during inversion.

The nonlinear inversion may employ Gauss-Newton, Levenberg-Marquardt, nonlinear conjugate-gradient, quasi-Newton, trust-region, alternating minimization, block-coordinate descent, variable projection, proximal-gradient, stochastic-gradient, expectation-maximization, adjoint-state, automatic-differentiation, or other iterative optimization techniques. Updates may be performed jointly for all parameters or sequentially for respective parameter blocks while retaining coupling through the joint objective function.

Convergence may be determined from one or more of: a magnitude of an objective-function change; a relative objective-function change; a residual norm; a scaled residual norm; a gradient norm; a projected-gradient norm; a parameter-update norm; a relative parameter-update norm; satisfaction of a statistical discrepancy principle; consistency between modalities; satisfaction of a constraint; an iteration count; an elapsed time; or detection of divergence or stagnation.

The modalities may include, without limitation, magnetic resonance imaging, X-ray computed tomography, positron-emission tomography, single-photon emission computed tomography, ultrasound imaging, photoacoustic imaging, optical tomography, diffuse optical imaging, electrical impedance tomography, magnetoencephalography, electroencephalography, fluoroscopy, mammography, elastography, thermography, or combinations thereof.

## Claims

1. **A system for reconstructing a representation of a subject from multimodal medical imaging data, the system comprising:**  
   an input interface configured to receive a first sampled dataset acquired from the subject using a first medical imaging modality and a second sampled dataset acquired from the subject using a second medical imaging modality distinct from the first medical imaging modality;  
   a memory storing instructions and respective forward models associated with the first and second medical imaging modalities; and  
   one or more processors configured, by execution of the instructions, to:  
   apply the respective forward models to a set of model parameters to generate a first predicted dataset and a second predicted dataset corresponding, respectively, to the first sampled dataset and the second sampled dataset;  
   scale at least one of the first sampled dataset, the second sampled dataset, the first predicted dataset, the second predicted dataset, respective residuals, respective objective-function components, or respective parameter updates;  
   construct a joint objective function comprising a first discrepancy between the first sampled dataset and the first predicted dataset and a second discrepancy between the second sampled dataset and the second predicted dataset;  
   perform a joint nonlinear inversion by iteratively updating the set of model parameters to optimize the joint objective function;  
   evaluate, during the joint nonlinear inversion, at least one convergence criterion; and  
   responsive to satisfaction of the at least one convergence criterion, output a reconstructed representation of at least one property of the subject.

2. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the set of model parameters comprises at least one shared model parameter used by both of the respective forward models.

3. **The system of claim 2**, wherein the at least one shared model parameter represents an anatomical boundary, a spatial support, a tissue classification, a material property, a physiological property, or a geometric transformation.

4. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the set of model parameters further comprises a first modality-specific parameter and a second modality-specific parameter.

5. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the scaling is based on at least one of a physical unit, a dynamic range, a sample count, a noise variance, a noise covariance, a signal-to-noise ratio, a residual norm, a Jacobian norm, a gradient norm, or an objective-function magnitude.

6. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the one or more processors are further configured to update the scaling during at least one iteration of the joint nonlinear inversion.

7. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the joint objective function further comprises at least one coupling term that promotes spatial, structural, statistical, functional, or parametric consistency between parameters associated with the first and second medical imaging modalities.

8. **The system of claim 7**, wherein the coupling term comprises joint total variation, a shared-edge penalty, mutual information, a cross-gradient penalty, a learned prior, a sparsity penalty, a tissue-correspondence constraint, or a probabilistic prior.

9. **The system of claim 1**, wherein at least one of the respective forward models includes an acquisition geometry, an instrument response, a sensitivity profile, a propagation model, an attenuation model, a scattering model, a relaxation model, or a noise model.

10. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the joint nonlinear inversion comprises at least one of a Gauss-Newton process, a Levenberg-Marquardt process, a trust-region process, a quasi-Newton process, a nonlinear conjugate-gradient process, a proximal process, an alternating minimization process, or a block-coordinate process.

11. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the iterative updating comprises jointly updating a plurality of model parameters based on derivatives of the first and second forward models.

12. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the iterative updating comprises alternating between a first update associated with the first medical imaging modality and a second update associated with the second medical imaging modality while retaining the joint objective function.

13. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the at least one convergence criterion comprises a threshold applied to at least one of an objective-function change, a residual norm, a gradient norm, a parameter-update norm, an inter-modality consistency measure, or a statistical discrepancy measure.

14. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the at least one convergence criterion comprises a plurality of convergence criteria having respective modality-specific thresholds.

15. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the first and second sampled datasets have different spatial resolutions, temporal resolutions, sampling geometries, physical units, or noise distributions.

16. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the reconstructed representation comprises at least one of a fused medical image, a quantitative tissue-property map, an anatomical image, a functional image, a molecular image, a segmentation, an uncertainty map, or a diagnostic indicator.

17. **The system of claim 1**, wherein the first medical imaging modality and the second medical imaging modality are selected from magnetic resonance imaging, X-ray computed tomography, positron-emission tomography, single-photon emission computed tomography, ultrasound imaging, photoacoustic imaging, optical tomography, electrical impedance tomography, elastography, electroencephalography, and magnetoencephalography.

18. **A computer-implemented method for multimodal medical image reconstruction, the method comprising:**  
   receiving sampled measurement data acquired from a subject using at least two distinct medical imaging modalities;  
   generating, using modality-specific forward models and a set of model parameters, predicted measurement data for the respective medical imaging modalities;  
   scaling data contributions associated with the respective medical imaging modalities;  
   determining respective discrepancies between the sampled measurement data and the predicted measurement data;  
   combining the respective discrepancies into a joint objective function;  
   iteratively performing a nonlinear inversion to update the set of model parameters based on the joint objective function;  
   testing at least one convergence condition during the nonlinear inversion; and  
   upon satisfaction of the at least one convergence condition, generating a spatial representation of the subject from the updated set of model parameters.

19. **The method of claim 18**, further comprising registering the sampled measurement data, the predicted measurement data, or modality-specific spatial domains to a common coordinate system, wherein at least one parameter of the registration is estimated as part of the nonlinear inversion.

20. **The method of claim 18**, further comprising estimating uncertainty associated with the updated set of model parameters based on a Hessian, an approximate Hessian, a posterior distribution, repeated sampling, or propagated measurement uncertainty.

21. **The method of claim 18**, wherein scaling the data contributions comprises whitening at least one sampled dataset using an estimated noise covariance matrix.

22. **The method of claim 18**, wherein the nonlinear inversion is terminated when a global convergence condition and at least one modality-specific convergence condition are satisfied.

23. **A non-transitory computer-readable medium** storing instructions that, when executed by one or more processors, cause the one or more processors to:  
   receive respective sampled datasets acquired by at least two distinct medical imaging modalities;  
   evaluate respective modality-specific forward models to generate predicted datasets from a set of shared and modality-specific parameters;  
   normalize contributions of the respective sampled datasets to a joint objective function;  
   iteratively update the shared and modality-specific parameters using a nonlinear inversion of the joint objective function;  
   evaluate convergence of the nonlinear inversion; and  
   output a reconstructed medical image or quantitative parameter map upon satisfaction of a convergence criterion.

24. **The non-transitory computer-readable medium of claim 23**, wherein the instructions cause the one or more processors to calculate derivatives of the modality-specific forward models by an adjoint method or automatic differentiation.

25. **The non-transitory computer-readable medium of claim 23**, wherein the instructions cause the one or more processors to modify a modality weight in response to a change in a residual, noise estimate, conditioning measure, or information measure during the nonlinear inversion.
